# AIGC in K–12 Classrooms: Global Applications, Evidence, Implementation, and Recommendations

AIGC—generative artificial intelligence that produces text, code, images, audio, or video—is already being used in primary and secondary education, but its educational value depends more on design and mediation than on the model itself. The strongest evidence in the supplied research comes from teacher-mediated or purpose-built tutoring: the two-year Tennessee KWiK trial improved mathematics achievement by approximately 0.06–0.08 standard deviations per school year, while the four-week Medly trial in English secondary-school science produced a preliminary Hedges’ *g* of 0.33. By contrast, unrestricted general-purpose AI use in one large Chinese secondary-school study raised homework scores while reducing closed-book examination performance. [Tennessee KWiK trial](https://edworkingpapers.com/sites/default/files/ai26-1551.pdf) [Medly evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14789) [Chinese secondary-school study](https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/generative-ai-learning-penalty-secondary-school)

The practical center of gravity is still teacher-facing: lesson planning, resource generation, differentiation, translation, assessment drafting, and administrative work. Student-facing uses are expanding through tutoring, inquiry, writing revision, coding, multimodal production, language practice, and accessibility support, but the evidence is much more uneven. A consistent finding across regions is that AIGC is most educationally defensible when it is grounded in curriculum and trusted sources, reviewed by a teacher, used to provoke student reasoning rather than replace it, and evaluated through independent performance.

This report therefore treats AIGC as a set of pedagogical approaches rather than a single intervention. It distinguishes measured learning outcomes from engagement and perceptions, separates generative systems from adjacent adaptive or conventional AI, identifies incomplete case fields explicitly, and compares primary and secondary, subject, regional, and implementation differences.

## Roadmap

The report first defines AIGC and establishes an evidence hierarchy. It then presents a classroom-lifecycle framework and taxonomy covering planning, differentiation, tutoring, student production, assessment, inclusion, operations, and professional learning. A global case-study map follows, with named systems and classroom examples. The later sections compare the mechanisms behind positive and negative outcomes, explain practical implementation and safeguards, examine future trends, and conclude with differentiated recommendations for primary schools, secondary schools, and education systems.

## Scope, definitions, and how to read the evidence

### What counts as AIGC in this report

The OECD and Fondazione Agnelli define generative AI as models that create new text, code, audio, images, or video in response to prompts, using patterns learned from training data. AIGC therefore includes large-language-model chatbots, text-to-image systems, code generators, multimodal generators, and educational products that embed these capabilities. [OECD and Fondazione Agnelli report](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/12/ai-adoption-in-the-education-system_43251cf0/69bd0a4a-en.pdf)

The boundary matters. An adaptive learning system that selects existing questions is AI but not necessarily AIGC. The report consequently treats Singapore’s Adaptive Learning System, Korea’s diagnostic AIDT functions, Finland’s metacognitive MAI, and CBSE’s Infinite Drum Machine as adjacent evidence unless the supplied source identifies generative content production. The CBSE lesson, for example, uses conventional unsupervised learning to cluster sounds and reports planned learning objectives rather than AIGC outcomes. [CBSE AI Integration Across Subjects manual](https://cbseacademic.nic.in/web_material/Manuals/AIIntegrationManual.pdf)

Some cases involve AI broadly but do not identify a generative model. Rwanda’s Wellspring Academy study reports AI-related benefits but does not name a generative tool; Semarang’s accessibility study names text-to-speech, digital writing assistants, and adaptive platforms but not a particular generative model. These cases are useful for transferability and inclusion conditions, but they are not treated as clean AIGC efficacy estimates.

### Evidence categories

The evidence base contains several distinct kinds of claim.

| Evidence type | What it can establish | Typical examples | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Randomized or quasi-experimental outcome study | A comparatively credible estimate of an intervention’s effect in a defined setting | Tennessee KWiK, Medly, Vietnam, sixth-grade science | Effects may belong to the combined program, not AIGC alone |
| Longitudinal administrative or quasi-experimental study | Associations or estimated changes over time in naturally occurring use | Chinese secondary-school study | Self-selection, one-region limits, and tool-specific conditions |
| Design-based or action research | How a workflow can operate and what participants produce | KiKo-Prim, Kapur, Mendes, LingoLift | Small samples, short duration, and limited controls |
| Qualitative case study | Teacher and student reasoning, interaction, agency, and implementation tensions | Norway, China, Indonesia, Korea | Analytical rather than statistical generalization |
| Survey or perception study | Adoption, confidence, perceived benefits, and concerns | RAND, DfE, Brazil, Portugal, TALIS | Self-report is not evidence of learning |
| Policy or practitioner account | Intended functions, safeguards, and operational experience | Korea AIDT, Singapore SLS, NSW NSWEduChat, Fulford | Often no independent outcome measure |

A 2025 systematic review of 134 AIGC-education publications found that theoretical work dominated the literature, with research concentrated in technology assessment, instructional application, learning outcomes, advantages and disadvantages, and future prospects. [Chen, Hu, and Wang systematic review](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10639-024-12549-7) A 2026 scoping review of 1,032 papers from four educational-technology conferences retained 189 empirical papers; GenAI publications rose from 5 in 2023 to 133 in 2025, but higher education remained the main testbed and longitudinal evidence remained limited. [2026 technology-research scoping review](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44436-026-00031-9)

A systematic K–12 review organized through the Presage–Process–Product model maps the field from learning goals and educational needs, through activities and collaboration among AI, students, teachers, and parents, to epistemic, practice, affective, identity, and ethical outcomes. Its categories include language and literacy, STEM inquiry, motivation, creativity, collaboration, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and AI literacy. [K–12 3P systematic review](https://doi.org/10.3390/systems13100840) The framework is useful for organizing evidence, but it is not a validated universal implementation model.

## An overall framework for AIGC across the classroom learning cycle

### From purpose to evidence

AIGC should enter a lesson through a pedagogical need, not through the mere availability of a tool. The central question is not “What can this model generate?” but “Which learning problem is difficult, costly, or inequitable to address without generation, and what human activity must remain central?”

A practical synthesis of the 3P model, Singapore’s platform design, the P-I-O-A proposal for junior-high English, the OECD learner–teacher–institutional model, and the Washington “Human–AI–Human” frame is:

1. Human beings define the learning purpose and constraints.
2. AIGC generates, adapts, simulates, translates, or analyzes material.
3. Teachers and students interrogate, verify, revise, and contextualize the output.
4. Assessment examines both the product and the learner’s independent reasoning.
5. The resulting evidence informs the next instructional decision.

This is a synthesis for practice, not a tested causal framework. Lu, Xiang, and Xie’s P-I-O-A model—Preparation, Immersion, Exploration, and Assessment—makes a similar proposal for interdisciplinary junior-high English. Teachers design, guide, verify, and evaluate; students experience, inquire, and reflect; AIGC generates content, contexts, tutoring, and assessment support. The authors explicitly state that their model had not yet undergone classroom testing. [P-I-O-A proposal](https://pdf.hanspub.org/ces_3096093.pdf)

### The classroom lifecycle

| Lifecycle stage | Human input | AIGC function | Required human judgment | Evidence produced |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Planning | Standards, learning goals, learner information, constraints | Generate ideas, sequences, questions, examples, or alternative representations | Curriculum alignment, developmental appropriateness, cultural fit | Reviewed lesson plan and rationale |
| Preparation | Trusted source texts, data, exemplars, accessibility requirements | Adapt reading level, translate, summarize, create visuals, generate variants | Factual accuracy, bias, accessibility, copyright, privacy | Approved materials and revision record |
| Instruction | Teacher explanation, student questions, classroom context | Simulate dialogue, provide hints, generate representations, support inquiry | Whether AI supports rather than displaces teacher–student interaction | Student questions, explanations, and participation |
| Practice and production | Student goals, evidence, drafts, code, experiments, projects | Offer hints, counterexamples, feedback, images, code suggestions, or role-play | Student agency, degree of assistance, productive struggle | Prompts, drafts, source checks, revisions, artefacts |
| Assessment and feedback | Rubrics, success criteria, student work | Draft comments, suggest questions, classify patterns, support self-assessment | Validity, fairness, tone, context, final judgment | Teacher-approved feedback and process evidence |
| Reflection and improvement | Independent performance, student reflection, teacher observation | Summarize patterns and suggest next steps | Whether apparent gains transfer without AI | Independent checks and revised teaching decisions |

The inputs, process, outputs, and accountability should be visible. A system that receives unverified prompts, generates opaque material, and produces a grade without teacher review has a different educational logic from a system that uses a curriculum chapter, generates draft variants, requires teacher approval, and asks students to explain and revise the result.

### Six application categories

| Category | Main purpose | Representative examples | Teacher role | Student role and central risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Planning and content generation | Reduce routine preparation and expand instructional options | NSWEduChat, Singapore ACP, ChatGPT, Gemini, Vietnam’s lesson design | Curriculum designer, verifier, editor | Usually indirect; inaccurate or culturally distorted material |
| Differentiation, tutoring, and practice | Adjust difficulty, provide hints, and expand practice | Khanmigo, Medly, Singapore ALS, Uruguay personalization | Set goals, monitor use, intervene | Learner or outsourced task completion |
| Inquiry, creativity, writing, coding, and multimodal production | Make students question, design, create, test, and revise | Fulford revision app, Xia’s maker curriculum, KiKo, AILIT, EDU-RELIGIA | Structure process and critique | Copying, shallow prompting, loss of authorship |
| Assessment and feedback | Generate questions, draft feedback, support revision and formative assessment | Singapore SAFA, Markly, AIME cases, Korean AIDT feedback | Define criteria and retain final judgment | Misleading feedback, invalid grading, reduced trust |
| Language, accessibility, and inclusion | Translate, caption, adapt, represent, and support communication | AILIT, LingoLift, Mendes, Semarang, AAC and accessible-math examples | Individualize without stereotyping | Privacy exposure, bias, inaccessible interfaces |
| Operations and professional learning | Reduce administrative work and develop teacher capacity | Appraiser, Sierra Leone’s TheTeacher.AI, Twiga, AI champions | Govern, coach, monitor, and learn | Fragmented adoption and unequal institutional capacity |

### Decision gates before choosing a use case

A school or teacher should pass seven gates before moving from experimentation to routine use.

First, the pedagogical gate asks what learning objective the activity serves and whether AIGC offers a meaningful advantage over a non-AI method. “Faster” is not enough if the saved time is offset by verification or if the task itself is where students need practice.

Second, the developmental gate asks whether the learner can understand the tool’s limits, protect personal information, and evaluate the output. Independent conversational use that may be acceptable for an older secondary student is not automatically suitable for a primary pupil.

Third, the evidence gate asks what kind of result is expected: teacher time, engagement, perceived confidence, accurate practice, durable achievement, independent transfer, or inclusion. These outcomes should not be substituted for one another.

Fourth, the grounding gate asks whether the output can be constrained by curriculum materials, trusted sources, local language, and explicit criteria.

Fifth, the human-review gate asks who will verify the content, feedback, or decision before it reaches a student or affects a grade.

Sixth, the equity gate asks who has devices, connectivity, accessible interfaces, language support, and an equally valuable non-AI alternative.

Seventh, the integrity gate asks whether the activity makes student reasoning visible and whether the assessment can distinguish supported production from outsourced learning.

## Global case-study map

The following catalog separates direct classroom evidence from policy, practitioner, and broader-AI evidence. “Unavailable” means that the supplied source did not provide the field; it does not mean that the field was absent in reality.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| **KWiK/Khanmigo, Hamilton County Schools, Tennessee, United States** | Grades 6–8; below-grade-level remedial mathematics; Khan Academy practice with Khanmigo; 2024–25 and 2025–26 school years; two years | Students attended daily 25–40-minute remedial sessions. MAP-linked placement structured practice and Khanmigo was configured as a coach; teachers supervised the combined program. | Two-year cluster-randomized field trial across 18 middle schools: +1.3 national percentile ranks per term, approximately 0.06–0.08 SD per school year, and an implied 0.14 SD for a full year of active participation. | Estimates concern the combined KWiK program, not Khanmigo alone. Controls used heterogeneous remediation, including adaptive software. In Year 2, 96% tried Khanmigo, but the median student messaged it on only one-third of practice days and in 17% of mistake sessions. |
| **Medly, English secondary schools** | Secondary GCSE Biology, Chemistry, and Physics; Medly AI tutoring; four-week evaluation submitted in 2026 | Students used Medly for revision; the comparison group undertook business-as-usual self-directed revision. The exact foundation model is unavailable in the supplied report. | Individually randomized multisite evaluation: 929 completed baseline testing and 644 post-testing. Primary ITT Hedges’ *g* = 0.33, with Physics 0.31, Chemistry 0.32, and Biology 0.52. | Attrition was 30.7%; outcomes were curriculum-aligned rather than standardized and process-evaluation response was limited. Findings are preliminary; greater engagement was associated with attainment but was not a causal estimate. |
| **General-purpose AI in one central-China county** | Grades 7–12; nine subjects; Doubao and DeepSeek; self-directed homework use from September 2022 to June 2025 | Students used general-purpose tools outside a guarded tutoring design. Teachers supplied adoption timing; administrative records linked homework, time, and examinations. | Longitudinal records for 26,811 students using staggered difference-in-differences: homework time fell from 64 to about 45 minutes, homework scores rose 18%, and monthly closed-book scores fell 20% after six months. High-school entrance losses reached 24% and college entrance losses 18% over roughly two years. | One county, general-purpose tools, and self-reported adoption timing. The study does not justify transferring the effect sizes to guarded tutors. The mechanism is consistent with outsourcing: roughly four-fifths completed work in under 50 minutes and had worse exams. |
| **Grade 5 mathematics, public school in Thanh Hóa Province, Vietnam** | Grade 5; circle circumference and area; ChatGPT v4.0, DALL·E 3, and Canva; one 35-minute mathematics period; implementation year not separately stated | Researcher and classroom teacher used backward design against Vietnam’s 2018 curriculum. ChatGPT drafted narrative and questions, DALL·E generated visual anchors, and Canva supplied interactivity; teacher reviewed every output. | Quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design with two intact classes and 30 students. The supplied findings document the workflow but do not report a measured learning effect. | The teacher rejected approximately 40% of initial DALL·E outputs, including culturally inaccurate Korean-style rice cakes and mathematically distorted shapes. Fixed classes and purposive selection limit generalization. |
| **Dynamic personalization in Montevideo, Uruguay** | Grades 4–6; ages 8–14; history and social science; ChatGPT-3.5/4, Midjourney, and Digileac; July 2023; one 15–20-minute test lesson per pupil | 110 pupils in four classes at two unnamed schools began with materials matched to initial knowledge groups. After questions, ChatGPT adjusted text complexity and questions; pupils were repeatedly regrouped. | After the first segment, 9.1% moved up, 73.4% stayed, and 15.5% moved down; after the second, 14.5% moved up, 44.5% stayed, and 41.0% moved down. Overall, 66.4% reported high enjoyment and 57.2% perceived much or very much learning. | No objective post-lesson learning measure was feasible. The case shows dynamic matching and engagement, not durable achievement. Teachers validated the source text, questions, and illustrations. |
| **Modern Public School, Shalimar Bagh, Delhi, India** | Classes VIII–X; English, science, social studies, and an interdisciplinary project; AI-enabled brainstorming and project work; ten weeks, one unit per week in 2024 | Ninety students and three teachers used brainstorming, research, group work, role play, presentations, reflection diaries, peer feedback, and real-life problem solving under direct teacher supervision. Exact AIGC model unavailable. | Action research reported mean academic scores rising from 54.82 to 76.91, a 22.09-mark gain, with *t* = 18.62, *p* < 0.001. Rubric scores also rose for creativity, critical thinking, communication, and collaboration. | Single purposively sampled school, no randomized control group, and a combined project-based/AIGC intervention. The outcome cannot be attributed to AIGC alone. |
| **Offline maker curriculum, rural high school in Hebei Province, China** | Grade 10; 50 students; interactive text-adventure game creation; Ollama offline engine, Open WebUI, and text-adventure templates; eight weeks in 2026 | A zero-cost, network-free progression moved from narrative basics to cultural multimodality, emotional companionship, ethical guardianship, originality, and meta-reflection. Teachers facilitated the maker process. | Researchers reported all AI-literacy dimensions with Cohen’s *d* > 3.2, *p* < 0.001, and 50/50 students completing games meeting preset standards. | One class, one rural setting, researcher-developed five-point scale, very low baseline, and acknowledged ceiling effect. The large effect sizes should not be treated as externally validated. |
| **Sixth-grade science lesson-planning study** | Grade 6 science; 100 students, 50 experimental and 50 control; teacher-facilitated GenAI lesson plans; exact model, school, country, and duration unavailable | GenAI was used by teachers to create structured tasks and multimodal resources within teacher-mediated 5E/constructivist instruction; controls received standard curriculum-based instruction. | Quasi-experimental pretest–posttest evidence reported significantly higher observed collaboration, science attitudes, and academic achievement gains in the GenAI-supported group. Numerical effect sizes are unavailable. | The source does not identify the model or duration, and the result may reflect improved lesson design and scaffolding rather than generation itself. |

The Tennessee and Medly cases are the clearest positive outcome evidence, but they also show why “AI tutoring” is not a single treatment. KWiK combined adaptive practice, MAP-linked placement, structured time, and Khanmigo. Medly was a purpose-built tutoring platform with a defined revision context. Neither is equivalent to opening a general-purpose chatbot and asking it to solve homework.

The Chinese study is the strongest warning against treating visible productivity as learning. Its homework and examination results moved in opposite directions, and its subject pattern was uneven: examination scores fell approximately 27% in social science, 22% in STEM, 17% in English, and 9% in Chinese. The authors’ mechanism is outsourcing, not a universal claim that all AI use is harmful. Students who continued to spend about as much time on homework as non-AI students had similar exam scores, whereas the fastest users had high homework scores and poor exams. [CEPR analysis](https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/generative-ai-learning-penalty-secondary-school)

The map shows why a single global verdict is misleading. The same broad promise—personalization—can mean dynamic text adaptation in Uruguay, a national adaptive pathway in Singapore, a guarded tutor in Tennessee, a digital textbook in Korea, or a teacher-created worksheet for a learner with a disability. These are different interventions with different risks.

## Comparing the major approaches

### General-purpose chatbot, purpose-built tutor, and teacher-mediated generation

| Alternative | Primary pedagogical role | Typical interaction | Best-supported benefit | Main failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| General-purpose chatbot | Explanation, brainstorming, drafting, answer generation | Student asks; model responds with broad knowledge | Immediate access and flexible support | Outsourcing, hallucination, weak curriculum fit, poor independent transfer |
| Purpose-built tutor | Hints, stepwise coaching, targeted practice | System follows a pedagogical script or curriculum path | Better alignment with practice and feedback; positive Tennessee and Medly evidence | Low engagement if the tutor is poorly integrated or students prefer direct-answer tools |
| Teacher-mediated AIGC | Drafting, differentiation, examples, visuals, questions | Teacher supplies goals and sources; reviews output before use | Scalable preparation and differentiated materials | Verification burden, inaccurate or culturally inappropriate output |
| Retrieval-grounded or institutional system | Curriculum-specific support and bounded answers | System prioritizes approved documents and may escalate unanswered questions | Better factual and institutional alignment | Narrow coverage, data governance, infrastructure and maintenance |
| Student co-creation or inquiry system | Questioning, testing, revising, producing artefacts | Student uses AI as a partner while documenting and critiquing interaction | Agency, creativity, explanation, and AI literacy | Prompting becomes superficial; generated product hides weak understanding |
| Offline or locally controlled model | Access where connectivity or data control is limited | Teacher or school runs a local model and templates | Potential equity and privacy advantages | Technical expertise, model quality, maintenance, and evaluation burden |

The comparison suggests that tool role is less important than the relationship among tool role, teacher mediation, and student incentives. A general-purpose model can support high-quality inquiry if the teacher structures source checking, counterargument, and reflection. A purpose-built tutor can still fail if it is imposed without classroom integration or if students use a more convenient unrestricted chatbot instead.

### Why task performance and learning can diverge

The Chinese secondary-school evidence explains the mechanism most sharply. Generative AI can improve the visible product while removing the practice through which learning occurs. If the assignment is intended to rehearse retrieval, problem decomposition, writing, or source evaluation, outsourcing the activity produces a misleadingly strong product.

The Tennessee trial illustrates a different mechanism. Its gains tracked realized practice time, with treated students averaging about 30 additional minutes of weekly Khan Academy practice and actively enrolled remedial students exceeding 45 additional minutes in Year 2. But the treatment bundled structured practice, placement, and Khanmigo, and most students used the conversational tutor only lightly. The positive estimate therefore supports the combined design, not a claim that more chatbot dialogue automatically improves learning.

Medly provides a related comparison in secondary science. Its positive preliminary estimate came from a defined tutoring platform and a short, supervised revision context, not from open-ended completion of assessed work. The appropriate conclusion is conditional: structured AI tutoring can improve post-test performance under some conditions; unrestricted answer production can harm independent performance.

### Primary and secondary differences

Secondary educators tend to use AIGC more often for assessment and student-facing work. In the English Department for Education survey, among GenAI-using educators, secondary use was higher than primary use for formative assessment—18% versus 6%—and summative assessment—16% versus 3%. [DfE educator and expert views](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/65b8cd41b5cb6e000d8bb74e/DfE_GenAI_in_education_-_Educator_and_expert_views_report.pdf)

A RAND survey using a broad AI definition found that 34% of secondary teachers compared with 18% of elementary teachers reported using AI for planning or teaching in 2023–24. The definition included chatbots, adaptive systems, and virtual assistants, so it cannot be interpreted as AIGC-only, but it reinforces the stage difference. [RAND 2025 teacher and principal survey](https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/research_reports/RRA100/RRA134-25/RAND_RRA134-25.pdf)

Primary practice is generally more adult-mediated and more sensitive to developmental, language, and privacy concerns. The Uruguay, KiKo, Mendes, and AILIT cases show that younger learners can question, revise, and create with AIGC, but only when teachers turn prompting and verification into part of the lesson. Secondary students can undertake more independent inquiry, coding, writing revision, and subject-specific critique, but they also have greater opportunity to use general-purpose systems for unauthorized completion. The Chinese secondary-school study, the Norwegian writing case, and the U.S. academic-integrity survey make that risk visible.

### Regional and cultural differences

Infrastructure and policy strongly shape what “AI use” means. Puerto Rico’s Khanmigo pilot was constrained by blocked Wi-Fi, five laptops for groups of about 20, construction, staff changes, and irregular IT support. Tanzania’s Twiga had to address curriculum misalignment and the abrupt transition from Kiswahili in primary school to English in secondary school. Indonesia’s student case depended on high smartphone ownership and affordable mobile data, while Hebei’s offline maker curriculum deliberately removed the need for network connectivity.

Cultural grounding affects content quality as well as access. In Vietnam, the teacher rejected DALL·E images that represented Vietnamese food through Korean-style rice cakes. Norwegian teachers described some generated language as Americanized and culturally vague. Chinese teacher cases showed that a model could perform well for meeting summaries but poorly for personalized feedback. These examples support a practical rule: local teachers must assess not only whether output is grammatically plausible, but whether it is culturally and pedagogically appropriate.

A cross-national TALIS analysis of 278,383 teachers in 55 countries and territories found substantially different perceptions of AI benefits and risks. Vietnam, Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, and Kazakhstan showed relatively high perceived benefit and low perceived risk; Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and Alberta showed high benefit and high risk; France and several Nordic systems showed lower benefit and higher risk. This is perception evidence, not classroom outcome evidence, but it cautions against exporting a single adoption narrative. [TALIS cross-national teacher-perception audit](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.08486v1)

The same study found that eight LLMs often overstated both teacher-perceived benefits and risks and compressed national differences. Country-specific prompting produced only modest improvement for some models. AI-generated summaries of “what teachers in a country think” therefore cannot substitute for direct consultation with teachers.

The supplied evidence contains no fully documented Middle Eastern school case with all requested fields—named institution, exact grade, model, duration, workflow, outcome, and safeguards. UAE-related studies appear in the broader literature list, but the supplied findings do not support a complete case card. That gap should be preserved rather than filled by inference.

## Category analysis: planning, content generation, differentiation, and personalized instruction

### Teacher planning and content generation

The most common practical use is to generate a first draft that a teacher then reshapes. In the 2026 RAND survey of 1,011 U.S. public-school mathematics and science teachers, 58% reported using GenAI for instructional tasks and 31% used it weekly or more. Among 588 users, 76% used it for instructional planning, 58% for assignments and assessments, and 57% for adapting activities for different learners. These are adoption and self-report data, not learning outcomes. [RAND 2026 teacher survey](https://www.amplifylearn.ai/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/rand_yr2.pdf)

The workflow is strongest when the teacher starts with a source and a constraint. Singapore’s Authoring Copilot allows a teacher to describe a lesson and upload a textbook chapter; the system proposes a structured digital lesson containing multiple-choice and open-ended questions, polls, and discussion activities. The teacher reviews and edits it. The tool’s value is therefore not “automatic lesson planning,” but accelerated drafting within a curriculum context.

The Vietnam Grade 5 case gives the clearest example of why review is necessary. ChatGPT generated narrative scripts and formative questions, while DALL·E supplied visual anchors. The classroom teacher revised the text for mathematical precision and age-appropriate vocabulary and rejected approximately 40% of the first image outputs for cultural or mathematical errors. A teacher who does not have time to inspect the output has not actually gained safe automation; the verification task has merely been hidden.

The Chinese teacher cases show that output quality depends on task fit. Lauren’s tools produced meeting summaries successfully in 78% of cross-artifact checks but succeeded in only 22% of personalized-feedback tasks. The numbers lack a reported denominator, so they should not be generalized, but the contrast is useful: a system can be reliable enough for formulaic summarization and unsuitable for nuanced interpersonal feedback.

The 2026 sixth-grade science study reported higher collaboration, science attitudes, and achievement in a teacher-facilitated GenAI lesson-planning group than in a standard 5E/constructivist group. The source did not identify the model, duration, or effect sizes. The plausible mechanism is improved instructional design—structured tasks, multimodal resources, and teacher-mediated scaffolding—not generation in isolation.

### Differentiated materials

Differentiation has three distinct forms.

The first is teacher-authored differentiation: generating several versions of a text, question set, example, or worksheet. This is the most accessible starting point for schools because students need not interact directly with an external model. Teachers can create a lower-language-load version, an extension task, a translation, or a visual explanation, then retain responsibility for choosing which version a learner receives.

The second is dynamic content adaptation during a lesson. In Uruguay, students were initially placed in advanced, intermediate, or basic groups, then regrouped after responding to questions. ChatGPT adjusted terminology, sentence complexity, examples, and questions while keeping the material length constant. Only 28.1% remained in the same knowledge group from beginning to end, showing how weak one-time placement can be. The finding supports dynamic checking, but the study measured within-lesson alignment and perceived learning, not durable transfer.

The third is adaptive sequencing, in which the system selects content and feedback over time. Singapore’s ALS creates individualized learning paths in upper-primary and lower-secondary mathematics and upper-secondary geography, adapting content, questions, and comments and giving teachers a dashboard. It offers hints or explanations after incorrect responses. This is a valuable personalization model, but it is not the same as an open-ended generative tutor, and the supplied case account reports no independent learning effect.

Korea’s AIDT plans combine all three forms: diagnostic data, personalized paths, dashboards, AI tutors, and teacher reconstruction of materials. The intended design also includes captions, multilingual translation, audio support, web accessibility, and multimodal content. Yet a nationwide survey of 132 elementary teachers found low understanding, concerns about training, field applicability, and reduced classroom interaction. The design promise and implementation readiness were therefore misaligned.

### Teacher judgment points

Teachers should check four things before using an AI-generated differentiated resource.

First, does simplification remove essential concepts or exposure to grade-level language? RAND cautioned that lowering reading levels indiscriminately may reduce access to appropriately complex text rather than improve learning.

Second, does the material preserve the curriculum’s intellectual demand? A simpler sentence is not necessarily a simpler idea, and an easier problem is not necessarily a useful scaffold.

Third, does the version reflect the learner rather than a stereotype? A model may infer ability from limited data or use culturally inappropriate examples.

Fourth, does the teacher have a way to determine whether the adaptation helped? The relevant evidence may be accuracy, explanation, reading fluency, recall, or independent performance—not simply time on task.

## Category analysis: tutoring, inquiry, creativity, writing, coding, language, and inclusion

### Tutoring and personalized practice

The core distinction is between an answer provider and a thinking partner.

Khanmigo’s Puerto Rico implementation illustrates a guarded design: the GPT-4-powered add-on withheld direct answers and guided students through reasoning and mathematical steps. The Tennessee trial similarly configured Khanmigo as a coach, although the message data show that many students did not engage deeply with it. Medly’s positive secondary-science result came from a purpose-built tutoring platform rather than an unrestricted chatbot.

The Finnish MAI pilot offers a small-scale example of metacognitive tutoring. Students aged 12–13 used the agent for one month in physics groups of three or four. MAI prompted independent problem solving rather than giving direct answers, and students reported more personalized assistance, discussion, group-work dynamics, and understanding. The source describes MAI as a metacognitive AI agent but does not explicitly establish it as an AIGC system or provide a controlled learning estimate. [University of Oulu MAI account](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1075204)

The Chinese general-purpose study represents the opposite incentive structure. Doubao and DeepSeek made it easy to complete homework rapidly. Students received high homework scores, but the efficient users showed substantially worse closed-book performance. This is not an argument against all student AI use; it is evidence that a system must make productive learning easier than substitution.

A practical tutor protocol should therefore require students to:

- state what they already know or tried;
- ask for a hint, question, worked analogy, or error explanation rather than a final answer;
- predict or explain the next step before requesting it;
- verify the tutor’s claim against a source, calculation, experiment, or teacher explanation;
- complete some work without the tutor; and
- reflect on what changed in their understanding.

### Inquiry and project-based production

Student-facing AIGC is most defensible when the product is not the whole task. The learning target should be question formation, source evaluation, design, explanation, revision, or reflection.

At Modern Public School in Delhi, students engaged in ten weeks of AI-assisted project-based work involving research, role play, presentations, reflection diaries, peer feedback, and real-life problem solving. The pre/post gains were large, but the lack of a control group means the evidence supports the combined project design rather than AIGC alone.

At Fulford School, students used Bing-generated code to build and test a multiple-choice revision app in 20 minutes. The activity gave students a concrete product, but its educational value depended on students designing, debugging, and using the app—not merely accepting generated code. In a secondary computing lesson, students should be required to explain the code, test edge cases, and modify it without AI assistance.

Xia’s rural Hebei maker curriculum used an offline Ollama deployment to move students through narrative, cultural, emotional, ethical, original, and reflective stages. Its importance is partly infrastructural: students could use a generative model without a network connection or subscription. Its reported effect sizes are unusually large and come from a researcher-developed scale with a low baseline and acknowledged ceiling effect, so the strongest transferable finding is the workflow and offline access model, not the numerical magnitude.

The EDU-RELIGIA case in East Java used AI as a “Thinking Partner” for argumentative Islamic Religious Education. Students moved from output-oriented use toward questioning, counterargument testing, and reflective revision. The case is small and qualitative, but it illustrates how a teacher can make the quality of the interaction—not the polished final text—the object of learning.

The Korean elementary pair-programming case similarly reports improved problem solving, engagement, and critical thinking about hallucinations among information-gifted students. The supplied abstract does not provide the country-specific school, grade, sample size, exact tool, or duration beyond identifying elementary gifted learners. It is therefore a promising but incomplete case.

### Writing and academic integrity

Writing is the area in which AIGC most directly challenges the assumption that a finished product represents the learner’s independent work.

In the Norwegian upper-secondary writing study, ten students worked on an essay analyzing song lyrics. Teachers instructed them to use Copilot for data-protection reasons, but six used ChatGPT. Video analysis found practices ranging from deliberate appropriation of generated text to substantial outsourcing, alongside new forms of agency. The study does not show that all students outsourced or that learning declined; it shows that a prohibition or tool preference does not determine practice.

The Norwegian teacher interviews reveal the resulting assessment shift. Teachers increasingly required process explanations, reflections on AI use, oral conversations, in-class work, and evidence of how students developed an argument. One teacher described AI as more suitable for assessment for learning than assessment of learning: students could receive feedback on a text, but the final product alone no longer reliably demonstrated independent thought.

A U.S. survey of 4,354 high-school students across six schools found that 72.06% reported at least one academically dishonest behavior in the previous month, a rate comparable to historical baselines. Students strongly supported AI for conceptual understanding and brainstorming, while 82.73% said completing an entire paper or assignment with AI should never be allowed. The authors caution that the sample was not nationally representative, that self-report can over- or undercount behavior, and that the cross-year comparison was descriptive rather than longitudinal. [U.S. high-school academic-integrity study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11423-026-10587-1)

The implication is not that schools should attempt to detect every AI-written sentence. Detection tools are unreliable and can be circumvented. A stronger response is to make learning visible through staged drafts, source notes, oral explanation, revision histories, supervised writing, and independent checks. Student disclosure should be normal rather than punitive: what tool was used, for which task, what was accepted or rejected, which sources were checked, and what the student changed.

The San Mariano National High School study supports this direction. Among secondary learners, information verification and disclosure of AI assistance positively predicted academic-writing integrity, while excessive reliance on AI-generated drafting predicted it negatively. The study is cross-sectional and does not test a disclosure policy, but it identifies a meaningful mechanism: integrity depends on how students use, verify, disclose, and integrate generated material.

### Multilingual learning and inclusive production

AIGC can remove barriers when it changes representation without lowering intellectual expectations.

In KiKo-Prim, multilingual Grade 3–4 learners used ChatGPT to retrieve vocabulary, refine explanations, and produce multilingual videos and podcasts. The interaction itself became a learning task: learners had to formulate prompts, interpret responses, and decide whether to adopt, modify, correct, or reject them.

AILIT extended this logic across borders. Students wrote in their first language, received AI translations and illustrations, read peers’ work in other countries, edited the translations, and revised their own compositions. The strongest enjoyment was associated with writing, but the study’s descriptive design cannot establish improved writing quality.

The Portuguese Grade 4 EFL case provides an important counterexample. The second AI adaptation generated the highest engagement but weaker vocabulary recall than the first. Engagement is therefore an intermediate indicator, not a sufficient outcome. Teachers need a balance of accessibility, meaningful challenge, retrieval, and repeated use.

LingoLift addressed autistic children’s oral-language learning by combining generated lesson plans and materials with teacher-entered language abilities and interests. Educators adapted content with gesture-recognition games, multisensory aids, and specialized autism-intervention strategies. The case illustrates complementarity: the model generated material, but teachers interpreted behavior and made real-time decisions.

The Semarang design-based study reported improvements in reading fluency, spelling, and written expression among pupils with dyslexia and dysgraphia across 15 elementary schools. Because the supplied abstract does not name a generative model or provide a student count, the case demonstrates an inclusive AI workflow rather than a clean AIGC effect.

Practitioner cases from Oregon, Kansas, and NWEA show related possibilities: an AI-enhanced augmentative-and-alternative-communication system for a student with cerebral palsy, image generation for autistic students who benefit from concrete visual structure, and an accessible mathematics prototype that lets blind students explore equations in segments rather than line by line. These accounts contain no controlled comparisons or effect sizes, but they emphasize that the teacher remains central and that accessibility must be built into the interface, not added after deployment. [K–12 AI accessibility cases](https://edcircuit.com/ai-and-accessibility-in-k-12-education-a-turning-point/)

## Category analysis: assessment, feedback, operations, and professional learning

### Formative feedback and assessment generation

The most defensible assessment use is formative and teacher-reviewed.

Singapore’s Short Answer Feedback Assistant asks the teacher to specify what a strong answer contains and how marks are awarded. It produces a draft comment and suggested mark, which the teacher reviews, adjusts, and approves before the student sees it. It does not mark mathematics requiring step-by-step working in the described implementation.

Markly, conceptualized by Singapore’s Ministry of Education in 2025, supported iterative feedback in geography, English, social studies, and history. At Canberra Secondary School, students were already on their sixth draft after beginning two weeks earlier. The teacher reported completing six rounds in three weeks rather than nearly a term, but retained final grading. A student said teacher explanations were more understandable than some AI feedback. The pilot was still collecting feedback and had not established outcomes.

Korean teachers using AIDT writing feedback reported technological support but also inaccuracy and limited customization, requiring additional review and modification. The pattern is consistent with the broader assessment literature: AI can increase feedback frequency, but speed does not guarantee accuracy, trust, or uptake.

A 2025 K–12 formative-assessment paper describes teachers as co-designers who use AI to unpack standards, draft questions, rubrics, feedback stems, and formative tasks. Its high-school English case reported increased revision cycles and engagement after AI-generated feedback, but the school, model, duration, sample, and effect size were unavailable. The same paper explicitly notes that human feedback remains superior in accuracy and tone in cited work. [AIME-Con formative assessment paper](https://aclanthology.org/2025.aimecon-main.12.pdf)

A review of assessment applications reports examples of automated question generation, rubric-aligned hints, essay and short-answer scoring, and multimodal handwritten-response evaluation. It also states that automated feedback requires expert validation and that multi-agent evaluation may reduce single-model bias. These are promising technical directions, not established primary or secondary outcomes. [Assessment review](https://doi.org/10.3390/info16060469)

### Redesigning assessment rather than automating old assessment

Assessment redesign should begin with the construct being measured.

If the goal is factual recall or independent calculation, the school should include supervised, no-AI opportunities to demonstrate it. If the goal is research, argument, design, or revision, AI may be permitted within a documented process, but the student must show source selection, decisions, drafts, and reflection.

The Brazilian K–12 science survey demonstrates why context matters. More than 400 teachers reported weekly exercise lists, monthly homework, regular in-person tests, and very limited online testing. Approximately half were neutral about whether ChatGPT would enhance educational quality, and opinions about whether its use constituted plagiarism were divided. This is not an AI intervention study, but it shows that assessment culture and teacher interpretation shape the practical meaning of any AIGC policy. [Brazilian K–12 science teacher survey](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2024.1321547/full)

A process-sensitive assessment package may include:

- a student-generated question or plan before AI use;
- a record of sources and prompts;
- an annotated comparison of AI suggestions;
- drafts and revision decisions;
- a short oral explanation or defense;
- a teacher-observed or closed-book component; and
- a reflection stating what the student learned independently.

This approach does not assume that every assignment must be oral or handwritten. It makes the permitted use of AI explicit and shifts attention from trying to prove that a product is “human” toward evaluating whether the student can reason, explain, verify, and transfer.

### Classroom operations and teacher workflow

Teacher-facing operational uses are currently more mature than student-facing ones. NSW teachers reported time savings in producing resources. Singapore’s Appraiser generated more than 40,000 testimonial drafts for over 4,000 teachers by early 2025, with teacher review and a fairness test on synthetic gender and ethnicity data. The operational scale is real, but neither case provides a student learning outcome.

Sierra Leone’s TheTeacher.AI shows how a teacher-facing chatbot can support lesson planning, classroom management, and subject knowledge across 122 schools and 193 teachers. Twiga shows the importance of local curriculum retrieval and mobile access, but also the need to address language and curriculum alignment before scaling.

Ofsted’s 2025 study of 21 early-adopter schools and colleges found that most used small steps, AI champions, approved-tool lists, policy integration, and protected experimentation time. A cited workload trial suggested a 31% reduction in planning and administration time, equivalent to 25 minutes per week, but Ofsted found no conclusive reliable evidence that AI improves knowledge. [Ofsted early-adopter report](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-in-schools-and-further-education-findings-from-early-adopters/the-biggest-risk-is-doing-nothing-insights-from-early-adopters-of-artificial-intelligence-in-schools-and-further-education-colleges)

Professional learning must therefore address judgment, not merely tool operation. In the 2026 RAND survey, 58% of teachers reported no formal GenAI training, 48% cited insufficient training as a barrier, and the most requested topics were lesson planning and materials creation, tool basics, and differentiation. Only 10% reported monitoring or reviewing student AI use on assignments. Training and policy exposure were more common among frequent users, but the survey is descriptive and cannot establish causality.

### Teacher and student agency

A 2025–26 global case pattern is emerging:

- teachers use AIGC most confidently for drafts, examples, and routine preparation;
- students prefer explanation, brainstorming, and revision support to full assignment completion;
- teachers become more cautious as tasks approach grading, authorship, or personal data;
- student use can outpace institutional guidance; and
- the most successful designs make verification and reflection part of the task.

The English DfE reported that teachers were more comfortable with teacher-facing use than pupil-facing use and recommended close supervision, filtering, and monitoring for student use. [DfE generative-AI guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education/generative-artificial-intelligence-ai-in-education)

## Practical implementation methods and safeguards

### 1. Begin with a bounded need

A school should first identify a recurring problem such as:

- insufficient time to create accessible examples;
- lack of opportunities for language conversation;
- difficulty providing immediate formative feedback;
- limited access to tutoring;
- barriers to communication or visual representation; or
- teacher workload in routine drafting.

The initial use case should be small enough to review manually and important enough to matter. Teacher-facing planning, source-grounded question generation, translation, and accessibility adaptation are generally lower risk than unsupervised student use in high-stakes assessment.

A needs assessment should document the current method, time cost, quality problem, affected learners, equity implications, and non-AI alternative. The question is not whether AIGC is impressive, but whether it improves the specific baseline.

### 2. Design prompts around curriculum and learners

A useful teacher prompt should specify:

- grade or age range;
- subject and curriculum standard;
- learning objective and prerequisite knowledge;
- language and reading demands;
- known misconceptions;
- local examples or cultural requirements;
- acceptable sources;
- output format;
- accessibility requirements;
- what the model must not do; and
- how uncertainty should be flagged.

The prompt should request a draft, not final authority. For a science lesson, the teacher might ask for three examples and two likely misconceptions, then verify every claim. For a writing task, the model might generate feedback questions rather than rewrite the student’s paragraph.

### 3. Ground the output in trusted material

Source grounding reduces—but does not eliminate—hallucination. Teachers should provide approved textbook passages, curriculum documents, primary sources, data, worked examples, or school-approved reference material. Retrieval-grounded systems such as Twiga and institutional-content platforms such as Noodle Factory illustrate this principle: the system prioritizes educator-curated material and can restrict or switch off broader model access.

Grounding should be followed by verification. The Vietnam teacher’s rejection of 40% of initial images shows that even a culturally familiar, visually simple topic can produce inaccurate output. Verification should cover:

- factual claims and calculations;
- quotations and citations;
- age-appropriate language;
- cultural and historical representation;
- bias and stereotypes;
- accessibility;
- copyright and licensing; and
- consistency with the intended learning objective.

### 4. Keep human review proportionate to risk

The teacher should review every student-facing output that could shape understanding, identity, safety, or assessment. Human review is especially important for:

- medical, legal, historical, or safety-related content;
- disability-related recommendations;
- culturally specific content;
- student feedback;
- grades or placement;
- individual education plans;
- emotional or behavioral support; and
- outputs generated from personal information.

Human review does not mean redoing every routine task from scratch. It means setting the criteria, checking representative outputs, correcting errors, and retaining authority for consequential decisions.

### 5. Make student use explicit and documentable

Students need a usable policy rather than a general warning. A classroom policy should distinguish:

- **permitted support:** brainstorming, explaining a concept, generating practice questions, translation, accessibility support;
- **permitted with disclosure:** drafting, revision suggestions, coding assistance, image generation, role-play;
- **restricted use:** tasks where AI can be used only after teacher approval or within a specified stage; and
- **not permitted:** unsupervised completion of a whole assignment, unauthorized use in an assessment, or submission of generated work as independent work.

A disclosure statement can be brief: tool, date, purpose, important prompt or instruction, material accepted or rejected, and student verification. Primary pupils may use a teacher-maintained log, oral explanation, or simple “what the AI suggested and what I changed” form. Secondary students should learn citation, provenance, staged drafting, and source verification.

### 6. Redesign assessment for independent transfer

Schools should not infer learning from improved AI-assisted products alone. Every sustained pilot should include at least one independent measure:

- a short no-AI quiz;
- a new problem or unfamiliar text;
- oral explanation;
- in-class writing;
- practical demonstration;
- code explanation and debugging;
- retrieval after a delay; or
- transfer to a different context.

The Chinese evidence shows why homework grades can become misleading. A rapid rise in homework scores paired with falling closed-book performance is a warning sign, not a success indicator.

### 7. Protect privacy, safety, and age appropriateness

UNESCO recommends data privacy protection and an age limit for independent conversations with GenAI platforms. [UNESCO guidance](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research) England’s guidance recommends not entering personal data into GenAI tools and states that original student work should not be used to train models without appropriate permission. [DfE guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education/generative-artificial-intelligence-ai-in-education)

Schools should:

- use approved accounts and data-protection agreements;
- avoid names, disability labels, behavioral records, and identifiable writing in open tools;
- check age restrictions and parental or guardian requirements;
- enable filtering and monitoring for student-facing use;
- explain data retention and model-training practices;
- provide a human route when a student encounters unsafe or incorrect content;
- prevent automated placement, grading, or disciplinary decisions without human review; and
- retain an accessible non-AI alternative.

### 8. Treat accessibility and equity as design requirements

A tool is not inclusive merely because it can generate a translation or image. Leaders should check keyboard access, screen-reader compatibility, captions, contrast, alternative text, speech input, reading load, device requirements, and the ability to export or preserve student work.

The accessibility evidence recommends tool inventories, vendor Accessibility Conformance Reports, WCAG 2.1-aligned procurement, annual review, and privacy and accessibility vetting before pilots. It also warns that AI can misinterpret dyslexic writing, non-standard grammar, speech differences, or disability-related communication. [AI and accessibility in K–12 education](https://edcircuit.com/ai-and-accessibility-in-k-12-education-a-turning-point/)

Equity requires more than supplying a login. Schools should provide devices, connectivity, supervised access, language support, accessible interfaces, and a non-AI route that does not disadvantage students who cannot or should not use the system.

### 9. Build professional learning around real lessons

Professional development should include:

- evaluating model output;
- writing curriculum-grounded prompts;
- recognizing hallucination and bias;
- adapting content without reducing rigor;
- designing student disclosure and citation;
- supervising younger learners;
- using AIGC for accessibility;
- redesigning assessment;
- protecting data; and
- examining evidence of independent learning.

The most effective format is likely collaborative: teachers bring an existing lesson, generate a draft, test it with colleagues, identify errors, teach or simulate the lesson, inspect student work, and revise. AI champions can support colleagues, but leadership should avoid making a small group responsible for all governance or allowing champions to become substitutes for formal policy.

### 10. Monitor outcomes and implementation fidelity

No validated universal thresholds currently establish when a school should expand, pause, or discontinue an AIGC intervention. Schools should therefore use a dashboard of indicators and make decisions against a predeclared baseline.

| Indicator | What to measure | Warning sign |
|---|---|---|
| Learning | Curriculum-aligned performance and independent transfer | Assisted work improves while no-AI performance declines |
| Agency | Student questions, explanations, revisions, and reflection | Copy-paste, one-word prompts, or inability to explain choices |
| Accuracy | Teacher error logs, factual checks, cultural review | Repeated hallucinations or systematic bias |
| Feedback | Uptake, revision quality, student trust, teacher corrections | Students ignore feedback or teachers routinely replace it |
| Equity | Participation, device access, language, disability access, alternative provision | Benefits concentrate among already advantaged learners |
| Workload | Preparation time, review time, administrative burden | Generation saves time but verification consumes more |
| Integrity | Disclosure, provenance, independent checks, unauthorized use | Rising unsupported products or unclear authorship |
| Safety and privacy | Incidents, inappropriate outputs, data exposure, vendor changes | Unreported or repeated privacy and safeguarding failures |
| Fidelity | Actual dosage, teacher review, student use, technical reliability | The intervention is not used as designed |

## Future trends and evidence gaps

### Multimodal generation

Multimodal generation is moving from novelty toward lesson authoring. A 2026 analysis illustrates a geography teacher generating an annotated tectonic-plates diagram, narrated animation, three-language voiceover, and formative quiz in under an hour. The same article distinguishes intelligent authoring, synthetic media for multilingual access, adaptive multimodal platforms, and multimodal language models, while noting that evidence of superiority over text-based teaching remains thin. [Multimodal pedagogy analysis](https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1828953)

The evidence already contains an important qualification. One controlled video experiment with 83 students found no significant difference between AI-generated and traditionally produced videos; another with 447 students found equivalent learning outcomes, while students preferred human-made videos for credibility and emotional engagement. Generation reduces production cost, but it does not automatically improve learning.

### Personalized tutors and metacognitive agents

Purpose-built tutors are likely to remain a major development area because they can constrain response style, use curriculum content, provide hints, and record interaction. The positive KWiK and Medly findings support continued experimentation, but the Chinese learning penalty shows that tutor design must address incentives. Students will often choose the path that completes work fastest unless schools make reasoning, verification, and independent performance consequential.

Metacognitive agents and multi-agent systems are also emerging. MAI uses prompts rather than direct answers; multi-agent assessment systems ask several models to debate or review one another. These systems may reduce some single-model errors, but no supplied longitudinal K–12 evidence establishes their cost, reliability, or learning effect.

### AI-enabled digital textbooks

Korea’s AIDT trajectory is the most important policy case. The national plan linked digital textbooks to personalized learning, inclusion, teacher facilitation, infrastructure, and large-scale training. The 2025 rollout then encountered technical, pedagogical, political, privacy, equity, and readiness problems, followed by reclassification as supplementary material.

The lesson is not that digital textbooks cannot work. It is that system-wide mandates can move faster than teacher understanding, procurement review, classroom testing, and public trust. Korea’s planned 2028 subject expansion is a policy milestone, not a forecast of successful adoption.

### Assessment transformation

A 2024 scoping review of 32 empirical studies, summarized in a 2026 multimodal-pedagogy article, identifies three levels of assessment change: students receive immediate feedback and self-assessment support; teachers need assessment literacy emphasizing critical thinking and integrity; and institutions must revise policy. [Multimodal assessment synthesis](https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1828953)

The likely direction is more process evidence, portfolios, oral explanation, authentic performance, and continuous assessment. But this transition creates workload, moderation, and equity problems. Automated feedback will require expert validation; oral assessment can be valuable but difficult to scale; portfolios can be more authentic but may create new privacy and access burdens.

### Teacher professional learning and governance

Teacher adoption is increasing, but infrastructure remains unstructured. In the 2026 RAND survey, 58% reported no formal training, 42% reported no formal district guideline, and 39% cited unclear guidelines as a barrier. At the system level, an OECD survey of 37 jurisdictions found AI mentioned in 26 of 32 responding strategies, but only eight strategies contained specific initiatives and six included timebound goals. [OECD education-system adoption report](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/12/ai-adoption-in-the-education-system_43251cf0/69bd0a4a-en.pdf)

UNESCO’s 2023 survey of slightly more than 450 institutions found that only 7% of schools and 13% of universities reported some AI guidance; around 40% of institutions with guidance said it was unwritten and communicated orally. [UNESCO policy survey](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-survey-less-10-schools-and-universities-have-formal-guidance-ai)

The likely near-term trend is therefore not fully autonomous classrooms, but the formalization of teacher-facing workflows, approved tools, platform-integrated tutoring, multimodal authoring, and assessment guidance. More agentic automation may follow, but the supplied evidence cannot establish a reliable adoption date, cost trajectory, labor effect, or long-term learning benefit.

### Evidence gaps

The most consequential gaps are:

- longitudinal primary-school evidence;
- causal comparisons of general-purpose AI, purpose-built tutors, and teacher-mediated AIGC;
- independent replication across languages and regions;
- disability-specific outcome evidence;
- cost and workload studies that include verification time;
- measured disclosure, citation, and assessment-redesign policies;
- evidence on family consent and independent use by younger children;
- learning-transfer outcomes rather than engagement or perceived learning;
- reliable monitoring indicators and expansion thresholds; and
- cases from underrepresented regions, especially the Middle East and rural or low-connectivity settings.

## Recommendations for educators and schools

### Primary educators

Primary schools should begin with bounded, adult-mediated uses:

- generate alternative examples, visuals, vocabulary supports, and multilingual materials;
- adapt teacher-approved texts while preserving grade-level concepts and intellectual demand;
- use short, guided AI interactions in pairs or small groups;
- ask pupils to compare an AI suggestion with a book, experiment, image, or teacher explanation;
- use AI to support accessibility only after checking the learner’s actual needs;
- keep personal data out of open tools;
- provide a non-AI alternative for every student activity;
- make children explain, draw, demonstrate, or retell what they learned without the system; and
- teach basic AI literacy through output checking, not through independent open-ended chatbot access.

The appropriate primary-school model is “teacher prepares, pupils question and create, adult verifies.” The evidence does not support assuming that younger pupils can independently manage accuracy, privacy, or authorship.

### Secondary educators

Secondary schools can use more ambitious, subject-specific approaches:

- guarded tutors for mathematics and science practice;
- source-grounded inquiry in history, geography, and social studies;
- writing revision based on drafts, feedback questions, and reflection;
- coding support combined with code explanation, testing, and no-AI debugging;
- language conversation and translation with attention to cultural and linguistic bias;
- multimodal projects in which the student remains the designer and editor;
- AI-generated practice questions reviewed by the teacher; and
- formative feedback that is disclosed, checked, and never treated as an unquestionable grade.

Every secondary department should define where AI is allowed in the process and where independent performance is required. Regular closed-book or supervised checks are necessary when homework can be outsourced. For high-stakes work, process evidence and oral explanation should supplement the final product.

### School leaders and systems

Leaders should:

- publish an approved-use framework rather than a vague ban or unrestricted permission;
- vet privacy, age appropriateness, accessibility, security, copyright, and vendor data practices;
- involve teachers, students, families, special-education staff, and local communities;
- appoint AI champions while retaining formal institutional accountability;
- provide protected, recurring professional learning;
- prioritize teacher-facing and low-risk pilots before student-facing scaling;
- establish procurement requirements for accessibility and data protection;
- fund devices, connectivity, translation, and non-AI alternatives equitably;
- define disclosure, citation, authorship, and assessment expectations;
- prohibit automated high-stakes decisions without human review;
- collect independent learning and equity evidence; and
- publish both benefits and failures of pilots.

A staged scaling strategy is safer than a system-wide mandate:

1. **Foundation:** identify a need, review privacy and accessibility, choose an approved tool, and define independent outcomes.
2. **Teacher pilot:** use AIGC for planning or materials, record time and verification, and inspect quality.
3. **Bounded student pilot:** introduce one defined student use with explicit prompts, disclosure, and supervised practice.
4. **Comparative evaluation:** compare assisted work, independent transfer, access, workload, and student agency with the previous approach.
5. **Scale or pause:** expand only when the evidence, safeguards, teacher capacity, and equity provisions are adequate.

### A concise decision rule

Educators should expand an AIGC use case when it improves a defined learning opportunity or removes a meaningful access barrier without weakening independent performance, teacher judgment, student agency, privacy, or equity. They should pause it when the visible product improves but learning transfer, accuracy, trust, or access deteriorates.

## Closing judgment

AIGC is neither a classroom replacement for teachers nor a single educational treatment. It is a flexible layer that can accelerate preparation, widen access to practice, support dialogue, and make multimodal production more feasible. Its educational value is highest when the teacher defines the purpose, the system is grounded in reliable material, students remain responsible for questioning and revision, and assessment checks what they can do without assistance.

The global evidence supports cautious expansion of teacher-mediated planning, differentiated materials, guarded tutoring, formative feedback, language support, and accessibility workflows. It does not support unrestricted substitution of general-purpose AI for practice, authorship, or independent assessment. The central implementation principle is therefore simple: use AIGC to increase the quality and reach of human teaching while making human reasoning, verification, and responsibility more visible—not less.
